description: //patch-automerge is extended here. FlareSolverr holds no state an upgrade could damage: browser sessions live in an in-memory dict in the process (src/sessions.py) and are gone on every restart, each session's Chromium profile is a temporary directory deleted when the driver quits, and the image's only VOLUME is /config, which nothing writes to unless LOG_FILE is pointed at it. This role mounts nothing there and configures no LOG_FILE, so a version bump is a pure image swap - no database, no schema, no migration step to run unattended on restart. Four patch spans were read to confirm that (3.3.24 -> 3.3.25, 3.4.2 -> 3.4.3, 3.4.4 -> 3.4.5, 3.4.5 -> 3.4.6): all of them are the Dockerfile's Chromium pin, package.json and small changes under src/, with no persistence code in any of the diffs.

The real risk a patch bump carries is that the Chromium it bundles moves with it, and a browser that cannot launch would leave a service answering HTTP while solving nothing. FlareSolverr exits non-zero when the browser cannot be found or started, so that failure shows up as a crash loop rather than as a quiet degradation - which `Restart=always` in the systemd unit would otherwise hide behind an `active` unit. The Molecule scenario is built around exactly that: it asserts the unit has not been restarting, and then drives a real browser through `POST /v1` - creating a session, fetching a page from a sidecar web server on the role's own container network, and requiring a marker the page paints in only from JavaScript, over a placeholder saying the opposite. Fetching the same page without a browser returns the placeholder, and a page the sidecar does not have returns neither, so the assertion cannot be satisfied by anything short of a working browser. None of that needs the public internet or a Cloudflare-protected site.

The scenario also asserts that the version the running process reports equals `flaresolverr_version` from defaults/main.yml, and separately that the running image's `org.opencontainers.image.version` label does. It runs on a non-default port and in a non-default timezone, both of which reach the container only through the env file this role renders, so an instance the role did not configure could not answer any of it.

What no offline test can see is a patch release that changes how well FlareSolverr does against a real Cloudflare challenge. That is a functional regression its consumers notice immediately and can pin their way out of, not a one-way data change, which is why it is not treated here as a reason to withhold automerge.

The tags support this too: ghcr.io/flaresolverr/flaresolverr publishes v-prefixed three-component semver (v1.2.0 through v3.5.0), so `patch` is a reachable update type - unlike the two-component streams elsewhere in this fleet, where `matchUpdateTypes: ["patch"]` can never fire. The only other things in the tag list are `latest`, a dozen `pr-<number>` build tags and three `-hotfix` one-offs; with `versioning=semver` on the annotation in defaults/main.yml, `pr-1234` is not a version at all and `v3.3.14-hotfix` reads as a prerelease of 3.3.14, so none of them can be offered as an update.
